content: 1. Psychosocial support, when provided early, adequately, and tailored to the needs of individuals and communities, plays a critical role in healing psychological wounds and rebuilding social structures following emergencies or critical events. This type of support can transform individuals from passive victims into active survivors. 2. Early and appropriate psychosocial support can prevent distress and suffering from escalating into more severe conditions. It helps individuals cope better, reconcile with everyday life, resume their regular activities, and address community-identified needs. 3. Supportive laws and policies are essential in shaping the availability and responsiveness of health services and programs to meet the needs and aspirations of individuals. These legal frameworks can influence the social and economic context, reinforcing positive social determinants of health and addressing harmful social norms or conditions that exacerbate health inequities. 4. Barriers such as the criminalization of consensual same-sex adult sexual conduct and other behaviors must be addressed. If these barriers persist, they will continue to impede access to health services, particularly following the use of self-care interventions. 5. Regulation is necessary to promote access to self-care interventions while ensuring quality and safety. This is a critical area of action to realize sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR). 6. Health literacy is fundamental for individuals and caregivers to make informed health decisions. Improving health literacy enables people to actively participate in improving their health, engage in community health actions, and hold governments accountable for health equity. 7. Enhanced health literacy allows individuals to better interpret, understand, and act on health information for improved self-care. It also helps them distinguish between accurate and inaccurate information, seek and assess the health information they need, follow self-care instructions, plan and achieve necessary lifestyle adjustments, make informed health decisions, and know when and how to access healthcare. 8. Digital literacy, which involves proficiency in using digital devices and platforms, is crucial when self-care interventions are delivered through digital channels. The uptake of such interventions may vary depending on individuals' levels of digital literacy. 9. People increasingly access health information, products, and services outside formal health facilities. Self-care interventions can be accessed through various avenues, including pharmacies, digital platforms (e.g., telehealth or mobile applications), health facilities, community caregivers, and traditional health practitioners. 10. Accountability in self-care interventions involves ensuring that government policymakers and other duty bearers fulfill their obligations to the rights holders affected by their decisions and actions. This includes shared accountability across local, national, regional, and global levels to support self-care interventions and ensure quality care and better health outcomes. 11. Self-care interventions should not function as standalone products or contribute to further fragmentation of the health system. Instead, they should be integrated into and supported by the health system to maintain accountability and ensure appropriate interaction and support for their implementation.
